text: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
reflection: In the ancient world, travelling at night was dangerous. Paths were uneven, and there were no streetlights. A traveller might carry a small oil lamp, which cast just enough light to see the next step or two. That is the picture behind this verse: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." Notice what it promises and what it does not. God's Word does not usually light up the whole road for miles ahead. It shows us enough to take the next faithful step. That can be frustrating when we want to see everything at once. But it keeps us close to the One who holds the lamp. This month we will think about God's Word and what it means to obey it. Begin by thanking God that you are not left in the dark. His Word lights the way. Open it today and let it show you your next step.
question: What next step do you need God's Word to light for you today?
prayer: Lord, Your word is a lamp unto my feet and a light unto my path. I do not need to see the whole road. Give me light for the next faithful step today. Amen.

text: Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee.
reflection: Where do you keep your most valuable things? Probably somewhere safe, close at hand, protected from loss. The psalmist treated God's Word that way: "Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee." To hide God's Word in the heart means more than reading it. It means memorizing it, meditating on it, and treasuring it so deeply that it becomes part of us. And notice the purpose: that I might not sin against thee. Scripture stored in the heart is protection. When temptation comes, there is often no time to look up a verse. But words already hidden in the heart rise up when we need them. Jesus Himself answered temptation in the wilderness by quoting Scripture from memory. Memorizing verses can feel difficult, especially as we get older. But even one verse a week adds up over time. Choose a verse today and begin hiding it in your heart. It will be there when you need it.
question: Which verse could you begin hiding in your heart today?
prayer: Lord, I want to hide Your word in my heart, that I might not sin against You. Help me store it deep, so it rises up to guard me when temptation comes. Amen.

text: This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success.
reflection: Moses had died, and Joshua now faced the enormous task of leading Israel into the Promised Land. God gave him many promises, and one clear instruction: "This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein." Before the battles, before the strategy, God told Joshua to stay in His Word. Meditating day and night means keeping Scripture constantly in mind, turning it over, speaking it, and applying it. And the purpose is obedience: that thou mayest observe to do. Meditation is not just thinking about God's Word. It leads to doing it. The verse ends with a promise: then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success. Real success, in God's eyes, flows from a life shaped by His Word. Whatever challenges you face today, start where Joshua started. Let God's Word fill your mouth and your mind.
question: What challenge today could you begin by letting God's Word fill your mind?
prayer: Lord, let Your word not depart out of my mouth, and help me meditate on it and do it. Shape my life by Scripture, and lead me in Your way today. Amen.

text: But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
reflection: Psalm 1 opens the whole book of Psalms with a picture of the blessed person. After describing what this person avoids, the psalm reveals what they love: "But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night." Notice the word delight. This person does not read God's Word out of mere duty. They enjoy it. It is not a chore to be checked off but a treasure to be savoured. Delight and meditation go together. We think about what we love. If you love someone, your mind returns to them throughout the day. The same is true with God's Word. When we delight in it, we find ourselves thinking about it at odd moments, in the car, in the kitchen, before we fall asleep. If Scripture feels dry to you right now, ask God to give you delight in it. Read slowly. Look for His character on every page. Delight often grows as we linger.
question: What would help your mind return to God's Word more often through the day?
prayer: Lord, I want to delight in Your law, not just read it. Grow my love for Your Word, until my thoughts return to it day and night. Amen.

text: And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.
reflection: Psalm 1 continues with a picture of what happens to the person who delights in God's Word: "And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither." The tree did not plant itself. It was planted, placed there with purpose. And its location makes all the difference. By the rivers, it has a constant supply of water. Its fruit comes in its season. Not all at once, not on demand, but at the right time. Growth in the Christian life works like this. We are planted by God, rooted in His Word, and nourished day by day. Fruit comes gradually and in season. Some seasons are for growing roots, others for bearing fruit. The person rooted in God's Word does not wither when hard times come. Their leaf stays green. If you feel like you are not producing much fruit right now, keep your roots in the river. In His season, fruit will come.
question: Where are you impatient for fruit, and how could you stay rooted in God's Word while you wait?
prayer: Lord, make me like a tree planted by the rivers of water, bringing forth fruit in its season. Keep my roots deep in Your Word, and let my growth come in Your time. Amen.

text: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness…
reflection: Paul wrote his second letter to Timothy near the end of his life. He knew he would soon be gone, and he wanted to leave Timothy with what mattered most. One thing was confidence in Scripture: "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness." Given by inspiration of God means God-breathed. Scripture is not merely human wisdom about God. It comes from God Himself. And because it comes from Him, it is profitable, useful in four ways. Doctrine teaches us what is true. Reproof shows us where we have gone wrong. Correction shows us how to get back on track. Instruction in righteousness trains us to keep walking rightly. Scripture is not only for information. It is for transformation. The very next verse says its goal is to make us complete, thoroughly furnished for every good work. Approach your Bible today knowing that God breathed it. Let it teach, correct, and train you.
question: How might you read your Bible differently today, knowing God breathed it?
prayer: Lord, all Scripture is given by Your inspiration. Use it to teach, correct, and train me in righteousness. Do not only inform me through Your Word; transform me. Amen.

text: For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
reflection: The Bible is not like any other book. Hebrews describes it this way: "For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword." Quick means living. God's Word is not a dusty record of ancient history. It is alive and active. It speaks into our lives today. It is powerful, able to do what it says. And it is sharper than any sword. A double-edged sword cuts deeply and precisely. God's Word cuts through our excuses and reaches the hidden places of the heart. The verse goes on to say it is "a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart." Scripture reads us even as we read it. It exposes motives we did not know we had. That can be uncomfortable. But it is the kind of surgery that brings healing. When you open your Bible today, come expecting it to speak. Let it search you. Allow its living words to reach the places that need God's touch.
question: What might God's Word be searching in your heart today?
prayer: Lord, Your word is living and powerful, sharper than any sword. As I read it, let it read me, and search the thoughts and intents of my heart. Amen.

text: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
reflection: Isaiah contrasts two things: the passing beauty of creation and the permanence of God's Word. "The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever." A field of wildflowers can be breathtaking. But within weeks the blooms fade and the grass turns brown. Isaiah says human glory is like that. Kingdoms rise and fall. Fame fades. Even the strongest among us grow old. Ideas that seem permanent in one generation are forgotten in the next. But God's Word stands. It does not wither or fade. It is as true today as when it was first spoken, and it will still be true when everything else has passed. This gives us something firm to build on. In a world of constant change, opinions, and trends, we have a foundation that will not shift. If you feel unsettled by how quickly things change, anchor yourself in what endures. Read God's Word today. It will stand when everything else falls.
question: What fading thing have you been leaning on that you could exchange for God's unchanging Word?
prayer: Lord, the grass withers and the flower fades, but Your word stands for ever. Anchor me today in the Word that never changes. Amen.

text: But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.
reflection: After forty days of fasting in the wilderness, Jesus was hungry. The tempter came and suggested He turn stones into bread. It seemed like a small thing. He was hungry, and He had the power. But Jesus answered, "It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God." Jesus was quoting Deuteronomy, where Moses reminded Israel how God had fed them with manna in the wilderness. The lesson then and now is the same. Physical food sustains the body, but we are more than bodies. Our souls need nourishment too, and that comes from God's Word. We are careful to eat every day. We would never go a week without food. Yet many of us go days without feeding our souls. Jesus shows us that God's Word is not optional. It is our daily bread. Make sure your soul eats today. Open the Scriptures and let God feed you.
question: Has your soul been fed by God's Word today, or only your body by bread?
prayer: Lord, I do not live by bread alone but by every word that proceeds out of Your mouth. Feed my soul with Your Word today, as surely as You feed my body. Amen.

text: But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
reflection: It is possible to hear a great message, nod in agreement, and walk away unchanged. James warns against exactly that: "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves." Hearing is good. We need to hear God's Word. But hearing alone can trick us into thinking we are growing when we are not. James compares it to someone who looks in a mirror, sees a smudge on their face, and walks away without washing it. What was the point of looking? God's Word is meant to be done. It shows us what to change, and then it calls us to act. The deception James warns about is subtle. We can feel spiritual because we know a lot of verses or listen to a lot of teaching. But knowledge without obedience is self-deception. The real test is what we do. Think about something God has shown you recently in His Word. Have you acted on it? Take one step of obedience today.
question: What has God shown you in His Word that you could act on today?
prayer: Lord, keep me from hearing Your Word without doing it. Show me one thing to put into practice today, and give me the grace to obey. Amen.

text: And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?
reflection: Jesus asked a piercing question: "And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?" The word Lord means master, the one in charge. To call Jesus Lord is to say He has authority over our lives. Yet it is possible to say the word without living it. We can use the right language, sing the right songs, and still go our own way when it comes to everyday choices. Jesus noticed that gap and named it. His question is not meant to condemn but to awaken. It invites honest self-examination. Where are we calling Him Lord with our lips while ignoring Him with our lives? Perhaps in how we handle money, how we speak about others, how we use our time, or how we treat people who are difficult. Calling Jesus Lord is easy. Following Him as Lord is harder, but far better. Let His question search you today. Then bring your actions into line with your words.
question: Is there something Jesus has said that you call Him Lord about but have not yet done?
prayer: Lord Jesus, I do not want to call You Lord and not do what You say. Search my heart, and bring my everyday choices into line with my words. Amen.

text: Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock…
reflection: Jesus ended the Sermon on the Mount with a story about two builders. Both built houses. Both faced the same storm. But one house stood and the other collapsed. The difference was the foundation. "Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock." The wise builder did two things: he heard and he did. The foolish builder heard but did not do. From the outside, the two houses may have looked the same on sunny days. But the storm revealed the difference. Storms come to everyone. Rain, floods, and winds beat on every life. What matters is what lies underneath. Obedience to Jesus' words is like digging down to bedrock. It takes effort, and much of it is unseen. But when the storm hits, it holds. Look at your foundation today. Are you building on hearing alone, or on hearing and doing?
question: Which part of your life is built on sand, and how could hearing and doing Jesus' words strengthen it?
prayer: Lord Jesus, I want to build my house upon the rock. When the storms come, let my life stand firm because I have heard Your words and done them. Amen.

text: If ye love me, keep my commandments.
reflection: Jesus spoke these words to His closest friends: "If ye love me, keep my commandments." He connected love and obedience in a single sentence. Love for Jesus is not just a warm feeling. It shows itself in how we live. And obedience is not cold rule-keeping. It flows from love. Think about how love works in human relationships. If you love someone, you want to please them. You care about what matters to them. You listen to their wishes and honour them. The same is true with Jesus. When we love Him, we want to do what He says, not out of fear, but out of affection. This also means obedience is not a way of earning His love. We already have it. We obey because we are loved and because we love Him in return. If obedience feels like a burden, the answer may be to spend time with Jesus and let your love for Him grow. Love makes obedience a joy rather than a weight.
question: How could your love for Jesus show itself in obedience today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You said that if we love You, we will keep Your commandments. Let my obedience flow from love, not fear, and let my love be seen in how I live. Amen.

text: And Samuel said, Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.
reflection: King Saul had been told to completely destroy the Amalekites and everything they owned. Instead, he kept the best of the sheep and cattle. When Samuel confronted him, Saul claimed he had saved them to sacrifice to God. Samuel's answer cut through the excuse: "Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams." Saul thought he could substitute a religious gesture for obedience. He did what he wanted and then tried to make it look spiritual. But God was not impressed. He does not want offerings that cover up disobedience. He wants hearts that listen and obey. We can fall into the same trap. We may give money, serve at events, or sing loudly, while ignoring what God has clearly told us to do. Those offerings cannot replace obedience. God is not looking for impressive gestures. He is looking for listening hearts. What has He asked of you? Doing that is better than any sacrifice.
question: Is there something God has asked of you that you have been replacing with a religious gesture?
prayer: Lord, to obey is better than sacrifice. Keep me from offering You gestures in place of obedience. Give me a listening heart that does what You ask. Amen.

text: And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart…
reflection: Right after the great command to love the Lord with all your heart, soul, and might, Moses said, "And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart." God's words were not meant to stay on tablets of stone or pages in a book. They were meant to live inside His people. A commandment written only on paper can be forgotten. A commandment written on the heart shapes everything. When God's Word is in our hearts, it influences our desires, our reactions, and our decisions. It is not something we have to look up. It is part of who we are. How does God's Word get into our hearts? Through reading, memorizing, meditating, and obeying. Each time we take it in and live it out, it goes deeper. Over time, His thoughts become our thoughts. Today, take one verse and carry it with you. Think about it while you work and rest. Let it settle into your heart.
question: Which verse could you carry with you today and let settle in your heart?
prayer: Lord, let Your words be in my heart, not just on a page. Let them shape my desires and my decisions, and keep me close to You today. Amen.

text: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
reflection: Moses continued with practical instructions: "thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." Faith was not meant to be passed on only through formal lessons. It was meant to be woven into everyday life. Sitting at home, walking along the road, going to bed, and getting up. Every ordinary moment became an opportunity to talk about God. This is how faith is often passed on most effectively. Not just in structured teaching, but in natural conversation. A parent pointing out God's handiwork on a walk. A grandparent sharing how God helped them through a hard time. A prayer before sleep. A verse at breakfast. If you have children or young people in your life, look for ordinary moments to talk about God today. If not, the same principle applies to friends and neighbours. Let God's Word come up naturally in everyday conversation.
question: What ordinary moment today could you use to talk about God with someone at home?
prayer: Lord, help me speak of You at home, along the way, at bedtime, and in the morning. Let my faith be passed on through simple, everyday conversation. Amen.

text: The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.
reflection: David begins Psalm 19 by describing how the heavens declare the glory of God. The sun, moon, and stars speak of His power. But then David turns to another kind of revelation, God's Word: "The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple." Creation shows us that God exists and is powerful. But Scripture tells us who He is and how to know Him. And it does something creation cannot do. It converts the soul. The word converting can also mean restoring or reviving. God's Word brings life to weary hearts. It turns us around when we are heading the wrong way. It refreshes us when we are drained. And it makes wise the simple. You do not need to be highly educated to gain wisdom from Scripture. God's Word is accessible to anyone with an open heart. If your soul feels tired today, go to His Word. Let it restore you.
question: Where is your soul weary, and how could God's Word restore it today?
prayer: Lord, Your law is perfect, restoring the soul, and Your testimony makes wise the simple. Restore my weary heart today through Your Word. Amen.

text: More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb.
reflection: What do people desire most? Money and pleasure have always been near the top of the list. David takes those two things, gold and honey, and says God's Word is better than both: "More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb." Gold represents value and security. Honey represents sweetness and delight. David says God's Word is more valuable than the finest gold and sweeter than the purest honey. That is a bold claim. Many of us would not naturally say it. We may treat our Bibles as worthy but dull. But David had tasted something real. He had found in God's words a treasure that wealth cannot buy and a sweetness that nothing else can match. If that is not your experience yet, ask God to give you a taste for His Word. Like honey, it is best enjoyed slowly. Read a passage today and savour it rather than rushing through.
question: What would help you savour God's Word slowly today instead of rushing through it?
prayer: Lord, Your words are more to be desired than gold and sweeter than honey. Give me a taste for Your Word, and help me savour it slowly today. Amen.

text: Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law.
reflection: Before reading the Bible, it is worth praying this simple prayer: "Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law." The psalmist recognized that he needed help to see. It is possible to read Scripture with our eyes but miss what is there. Our minds wander. Our hearts are distracted. Familiar passages become routine. We need God to open our eyes. The psalmist also expected to find wonders. Wondrous things. He did not approach God's Word as a textbook to be studied or a rulebook to be obeyed, though it teaches and commands. He approached it as a treasure chest full of marvels. God's character, His promises, His works, and His love are all there, waiting to be discovered. Many people have read a verse dozens of times and then suddenly seen something new. That is God opening their eyes. Pray this prayer before you read today. Then read with expectation. There are wonders waiting.
question: What wonder might you see in Scripture today if you read expecting God to open your eyes?
prayer: Lord, open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of Your law. I cannot see them on my own. Show me the marvels of Your Word today. Amen.

text: The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
reflection: When you step into a dark room and flip a switch, light floods in all at once. The psalmist describes God's Word in a similar way: "The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple." The entrance of thy words. When God's Word enters a heart, a mind, or a situation, light comes in. Confusion clears. What was hidden becomes visible. We begin to see ourselves, our circumstances, and God more clearly. And this light is for the simple. Not only scholars or experts. The word simple here describes someone open and teachable, perhaps inexperienced. God's Word is not locked away for a select few. It gives understanding to anyone willing to receive it. If you feel confused about a decision, a relationship, or your own heart, let God's Word in. Open the door and let it shine. You may be surprised at how much becomes clear when His light enters.
question: What feels unclear in your life right now that you could bring into the light of God's Word?
prayer: Lord, the entrance of Your words gives light and understanding to the simple. Shine Your Word into what feels confused in my life, and give me understanding. Amen.

text: Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart: for I am called by thy name, O LORD God of hosts.
reflection: Jeremiah had a hard calling. He was mocked, beaten, and imprisoned for speaking God's message. Yet he wrote this: "Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart." Jeremiah did not just read God's words. He ate them. He took them in so fully that they became part of him. And the result was joy, even in a life full of hardship. His circumstances were often miserable. But God's Word was his joy and the rejoicing of his heart. This shows us something important. Joy does not depend on having an easy life. It can come from feeding on God's Word in the middle of difficulty. Jeremiah also gives the reason: "for I am called by thy name, O LORD God of hosts." He belonged to God, and God's words were his nourishment. Feed on God's Word today, especially if life is hard. Let it become the joy of your heart.
question: In a hard season, how could you take in God's Word deeply enough for it to become your joy?
prayer: Lord, Your words were found, and I did eat them, and they became the joy of my heart. Even in hardship, let Your Word nourish me and fill me with joy. Amen.

text: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
reflection: When Paul and Silas preached in the city of Berea, the people there responded in a way that earned them praise: "they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so." The Bereans did two things. First, they were eager. They received the message with open hearts. Second, they checked it against Scripture. They did not simply accept everything they heard, even from an apostle. They went to God's Word to confirm it. This is a healthy model. Openness and discernment go together. We should be eager to learn, but we should test what we hear against the Bible. In a world full of voices, teachers, podcasts, and opinions, this matters more than ever. Not everything that sounds spiritual is true. The Bereans searched the Scriptures daily. It was a habit, not an occasional activity. Follow their example today. Listen eagerly, but check everything against God's Word.
question: What have you heard lately that you could test carefully against God's Word?
prayer: Lord, give me an eager heart to receive Your truth, and a careful mind to search the Scriptures. Help me hold together openness and discernment. Amen.

text: Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
reflection: Jesus spoke these words to religious leaders who knew the Scriptures well. They studied them carefully and memorized large portions. Yet Jesus said, "Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me." They had missed the point. The Scriptures were not an end in themselves. They pointed to Someone. The whole Bible, from beginning to end, testifies of Jesus. The promises, prophecies, sacrifices, and stories all point toward Him. These leaders had the map but refused to go to the destination. This is a warning for anyone who reads the Bible. It is possible to know a great deal of Scripture and still not know Christ. The goal of Bible reading is not just information, but relationship with Jesus. As you read God's Word today, look for Him. Ask how this passage points to Jesus or reveals His character. Let the Scriptures lead you to Him.
question: How could you look for Jesus as you read God's Word today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, the Scriptures testify of You. Keep me from reading for knowledge alone. Show me Yourself in Your Word, and draw me to come to You. Amen.

text: So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
reflection: Where does faith come from? Paul gives a clear answer: "So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God." Faith is not something we manufacture by trying harder to believe. It grows as we hear God's Word. When we hear what God has said and done, our trust in Him is built. In Paul's day, most people heard Scripture read aloud rather than reading it privately. The principle is the same today. Whether we read, listen, or study, exposure to God's Word strengthens faith. If your faith feels weak, the answer is not to stir up more emotion. It is to feed on God's Word. Listen to His promises. Hear His stories of faithfulness. Let His truth speak louder than your doubts. This verse also reminds us why sharing God's Word matters. Others come to faith by hearing it too. Today, take in God's Word, and look for a chance to share it with someone else.
question: If your faith feels weak, how could you feed it with God's Word today, and with whom could you share it?
prayer: Lord, faith comes by hearing, and hearing by Your word. Where my faith feels weak, strengthen it through Scripture, and help me share Your word with someone else. Amen.

text: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
reflection: Paul urged Timothy to work hard at understanding God's Word: "Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth." Study here means be diligent, make every effort. Understanding Scripture well takes work. It is not something we drift into. Paul uses the picture of a workman, someone skilled in a trade who takes pride in doing the job right. A good craftsman is not ashamed of his work because he has done it with care. Rightly dividing means handling accurately, cutting straight. It pictures a builder cutting a straight line or a farmer ploughing a straight furrow. We are to handle God's Word carefully, not twisting it to say what we want, not pulling verses out of context, but seeking what God actually means. This is not just for pastors. Every believer can grow in handling Scripture well. Read with care today. Ask what the passage meant then and what it means now.
question: What passage could you read more carefully today to understand what God actually means?
prayer: Lord, help me study Your Word with diligence and care, as a workman who needs not to be ashamed. Keep me from careless reading, and lead me into Your truth. Amen.

text: For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments.
reflection: Ezra was a scribe and priest who led a group of exiles back to Jerusalem. He became a key figure in renewing the people's faith. The secret of his influence is summed up in one verse: "For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments." Notice the order. First, he prepared his heart. Then he sought God's law, studying it carefully. Then he did it, obeying what he learned. And only then did he teach it to others. Many people want to skip to teaching. But Ezra knew that what we teach must first be lived. His teaching had power because it came from a life that had studied and obeyed. Preparing the heart means coming to God's Word humbly and ready to change. Whatever influence you have, as a parent, friend, or leader, follow Ezra's order. Seek, do, then teach.
question: Is there something you teach or tell others that you need to live out more fully first?
prayer: Lord, prepare my heart as You prepared Ezra's, to seek Your law, to do it, and then to teach it. Let what I say to others first be true in my own life. Amen.

text: So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
reflection: The walls of Jerusalem had been rebuilt, and the people gathered in the square. Ezra stood on a wooden platform and read from the book of the law from early morning until midday. But reading alone was not enough. "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading." The Levites moved among the people, explaining what the words meant. Many had returned from exile and may not have fully understood the Hebrew. They needed help. And when understanding came, the people wept, then rejoiced. God's Word is meant to be understood. Reading the words is important, but grasping their meaning is what changes lives. That is why good teaching matters, and why asking questions is healthy. If a passage confuses you, do not just skip over it. Seek understanding. Ask someone who knows more, use trusted resources, and pray for insight. Understanding God's Word leads to both conviction and joy.
question: Is there a passage that confuses you, and who could help you understand it?
prayer: Lord, I want not only to hear Your Word but to understand it. Give me wisdom and good teachers, and help me make Your Word clear to others too. Amen.

text: So Abram departed, as the LORD had spoken unto him; and Lot went with him: and Abram was seventy and five years old when he departed out of Haran.
reflection: God told Abram to leave his country, his relatives, and his father's house, and go to a land He would show him. It was a staggering request. Abram was settled. He had family and possessions. And God did not give him a map. Yet the response is told in a single sentence: "So Abram departed, as the LORD had spoken unto him." No recorded arguments. No delay. He went. And then we learn a surprising detail: "Abram was seventy and five years old when he departed out of Haran." He was not a young man looking for adventure. He was well into his years, with every reason to stay put. Some people think it is too late for them to follow God into something new. Abram proves otherwise. Age is no barrier to obedience. God calls people at every stage of life. Is God asking you to step out in some way? Whatever your age, you can still respond as Abram did. Go as the Lord has spoken.
question: What is God asking of you at this stage of your life, whatever your age?
prayer: Lord, Abram departed as You had spoken, even at seventy-five. Whatever my age or stage of life, help me respond to Your call with ready obedience. Amen.

text: By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.
reflection: The book of Hebrews looks back on Abraham's journey and highlights what made it so remarkable: "By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went." Not knowing whither he went. Abraham obeyed without knowing where he was going. He did not have a destination on a map, just a promise and a God he trusted. Most of us prefer to see the whole plan before we commit. We want details, guarantees, and a clear path. But faith often means taking the next step without seeing the end. Obedience is not always about understanding. Sometimes it is simply about trusting. Abraham went because he knew the One who called him, even though he did not know the place. If God is leading you somewhere unfamiliar, you do not need to see the whole road. You only need to know the One who is leading.
question: Where is God asking you to step forward without seeing where the road leads?
prayer: Lord, by faith Abraham went out, not knowing where he went. When I cannot see the road ahead, help me trust You and take the step You ask of me. Amen.

text: His mother saith unto the servants, Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.
reflection: At a wedding in Cana, the wine ran out. It was an embarrassing problem for the host family. Mary, the mother of Jesus, brought the problem to Him. Then she turned to the servants and said simply, "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it." What Jesus then told them must have seemed strange. Fill six large stone jars with water. Then draw some out and take it to the master of the feast. The servants obeyed. And the water became wine, the best wine of the whole celebration. Mary's words are some of the wisest in Scripture. She did not tell Jesus what to do. She told the servants to do whatever He said. That is the heart of obedience. We bring our problems to Jesus, and then we do what He tells us, even when it does not make sense. The miracle came through ordinary obedience: filling jars with water. Whatever He says to you today, do it.
question: What problem could you bring to Jesus today, ready to do whatever He tells you?
prayer: Lord Jesus, I bring my need to You, and I am ready to do whatever You say, even when it seems strange. Work in my life as You did at Cana. Amen.

text: And Simon answering said unto him, Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net.
reflection: Peter and his partners had fished all night and caught nothing. They were tired and cleaning their nets when Jesus got into Peter's boat and taught the crowd. Afterward, He told Peter to push out into deep water and let down the nets. Peter was an experienced fisherman. He knew the best time to fish was at night, and they had already failed. But he answered, "Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net." Nevertheless. That word turned the story. Peter's experience said it would not work. His tiredness said it was pointless. But Jesus had spoken, so he obeyed. The catch was so large that the nets began to break. This month we have thought about God's Word and obedience. End it with Peter's word. When your experience, logic, or weariness says otherwise, say nevertheless. At His word, let down the net.
question: Where is weariness or past experience keeping you from obeying what Jesus says?
prayer: Lord Jesus, even when I am weary and nothing has worked, I will say, nevertheless at Your word. Help me obey You and trust You with the results. Amen.
